variants.title: Operate the measurement system
variants.context: A world knowledge benchmark is operated in four stages: freeze product-shaped slices, run one traceable pipeline, attribute every failure to a stage before tuning, then gate the release with multiple signals together. Tuning before attribution fixes the wrong stage.
variants.prompt: A support assistant answers questions over a help-center corpus. Put the evaluation stages in order, from the first sampling decision to the release decision.

items.text: Gate the release on critical-slice floors, retrieval coverage, answer quality, no-answer behavior, cost, latency, and contamination together.
Attribute each failure to corpus gaps, retrieval misses, reader errors, alias failures, unsupported answers, or justified abstention.
Freeze product-shaped slices: stable facts, time-sensitive facts, ambiguous queries, answerable and unsupported questions in declared proportions.
Run one traceable pipeline that persists retrieval and reader inputs, outputs, versions, timings, and policy decisions for every item.

variants.hint: Nothing can be attributed until the pipeline has recorded what each stage received and produced.
variants.explanation: Scope, measure, diagnose, release: attribution needs a traceable run, and the gate needs attributed evidence.

variants.title: Operate the measurement system
variants.context: A world knowledge benchmark is operated in four stages: freeze product-shaped slices, run one traceable pipeline, attribute every failure to a stage before tuning, then gate the release with multiple signals together. Tuning before attribution fixes the wrong stage.
variants.prompt: An internal-document reader shows a lower exact-match score after a corpus refresh. The team wants to retune the reader immediately. Put the steps in the order the lesson requires, including the reader change.

items.text: Gate the release with critical-slice floors, retrieval coverage, no-answer behavior, cost, and latency together.
Freeze the product-shaped slices, including time-sensitive facts that the refresh should have changed.
Run the traceable pipeline over the frozen slices and persist retrieval and reader evidence per item.
Change the reader only if reader errors are the largest attributed bucket.
Attribute the drop by stage and check whether retrieval misses or reader errors grew.

variants.hint: Attribute before tuning: the reader is only the fix if the reader owns the failure.
variants.explanation: The pipeline attributes the drop to a stage before any tuning, so a retrieval regression is not misdiagnosed as a reader problem.

variants.title: Operate the measurement system
variants.context: A world knowledge benchmark is operated in four stages: freeze product-shaped slices, run one traceable pipeline, attribute every failure to a stage before tuning, then gate the release with multiple signals together. Tuning before attribution fixes the wrong stage.
variants.prompt: A closed-book trivia feature is compared with a retrieval-backed variant. Attribution shows retrieval misses are the largest bucket. Put the steps in order, ending with the next experiment.

items.text: Run both variants through one traceable pipeline with the same frozen slices.
Freeze slices that reflect the closed-book trivia claim rather than a retrieval claim.
Choose the next experiment on retrieval coverage because retrieval misses dominate.
Assign every question to exactly one outcome bucket so the largest failure source is visible.

variants.hint: The largest attributed bucket identifies the next experiment.
variants.explanation: Every question sits in one bucket, so the largest bucket, here retrieval misses, tells the team which stage to work on next.

variants.title: Score one retrieval QA item
variants.context: For one question in an end-to-end retrieval pipeline, retrieval runs first, the accepted answer is checked against the retrieved set, the reader answers, the prediction is normalized and scored against every documented alias, and the item lands in exactly one outcome bucket. Empty predictions count as abstention only on unanswerable items.
variants.prompt: An answerable TriviaQA question with three documented aliases enters the pipeline. Put the scoring steps in order.

items.text: Assign the question to one outcome bucket and persist the query, document IDs, raw answer, and scorer revision.
Normalize only documented surface differences and score against all three aliases for exact match and token F1.
Retrieve the top-k documents from the declared corpus revision.
Check whether any accepted alias appears in the retrieved set and record retrieval recall.
Have the reader produce an answer from the retrieved evidence.

variants.hint: The reader cannot be scored before it has evidence, and evidence cannot be judged before it is retrieved.
variants.explanation: Retrieval, coverage check, reading, alias-aware scoring, then bucket assignment: each step needs the record left by the one before it.

variants.title: Score one retrieval QA item
variants.context: For one question in an end-to-end retrieval pipeline, retrieval runs first, the accepted answer is checked against the retrieved set, the reader answers, the prediction is normalized and scored against every documented alias, and the item lands in exactly one outcome bucket. Empty predictions count as abstention only on unanswerable items.
variants.prompt: A SQuAD 2.0 unanswerable question arrives with its passage. The reader returns an empty prediction. Put the steps in order, ending with the bucket.

items.text: Record the empty prediction as the reader's answer.
Supply the bounded passage to the reader; there is no retrieval stage in passage QA.
Compare the reader's best span score with its no-answer score under the frozen threshold.
Assign the item to the correct-abstention bucket and report it in the unanswerable subset.
Confirm the item is unanswerable so the empty prediction counts as abstention rather than a miss.

variants.hint: An empty answer is right or wrong depending on the item's gold status, which must be checked.
variants.explanation: In passage QA the reader compares span and no-answer scores under a frozen threshold, and an empty prediction is a correct abstention only because the item is unanswerable.

variants.title: Score one retrieval QA item
variants.context: For one question in an end-to-end retrieval pipeline, retrieval runs first, the accepted answer is checked against the retrieved set, the reader answers, the prediction is normalized and scored against every documented alias, and the item lands in exactly one outcome bucket. Empty predictions count as abstention only on unanswerable items.
variants.prompt: An answerable Natural Questions item enters the pipeline, but no accepted alias appears in the retrieved top-k. The reader still guesses. Put the steps in order, ending with the bucket.

items.text: Score the raw answer against the aliases for the record, but mark it unsupported by retrieved evidence.
Let the reader answer and persist the raw answer without silently retrying.
Assign the question to the retrieval-miss bucket, not the reader-error bucket.
Retrieve the top-k documents from the declared corpus revision.
Check the retrieved set for an accepted alias and record a retrieval miss.

variants.hint: Which stage owns a failure when the evidence never arrived?
variants.explanation: A retrieval miss is attributed to retrieval even if the reader answers; the reader cannot extract evidence it was never supplied.

variants.title: Multiply the stages
variants.context: In a simplified retrieval pipeline, supported correct rate = retrieval recall x reader correctness given retrieved evidence. Improving only the reader cannot recover the questions whose evidence never arrived.
variants.prompt: Retrieval recall is 75 percent and the reader is correct on 80 percent of retrieved cases. What supported-correct rate can the pipeline reach on answerable questions, in percent?
variants.hint: The stages multiply; they do not average.
variants.explanation: 0.75 x 0.80 = 0.60, so at most 60 percent of answerable items are supported correct.

mistakes.feedback: That averages the two stages; a question must pass both, so the rates multiply.
That reports reader correctness alone and ignores the 25 percent of questions whose evidence never arrived.

variants.title: Multiply the stages
variants.context: In a simplified retrieval pipeline, supported correct rate = retrieval recall x reader correctness given retrieved evidence. Improving only the reader cannot recover the questions whose evidence never arrived.
variants.prompt: An evaluation has 1,000 answerable questions. Retrieval recall is 70 percent and the reader is correct on 90 percent of retrieved cases. How many questions land in the reader-error bucket?
variants.hint: Reader errors only happen on questions where retrieval succeeded.
variants.explanation: Retrieval supplies 700 questions; the reader misses 10 percent of those, so 70 are reader errors while 300 are retrieval misses.

mistakes.feedback: That applies the 10 percent reader error rate to all 1,000 questions, including the 300 the reader never saw with evidence.
That is the retrieval-miss bucket, not the reader-error bucket.

variants.title: Multiply the stages
variants.context: In a simplified retrieval pipeline, supported correct rate = retrieval recall x reader correctness given retrieved evidence. Improving only the reader cannot recover the questions whose evidence never arrived.
variants.prompt: A product claim needs an 81 percent supported-correct rate on answerable questions. The reader is correct on 90 percent of retrieved cases. What retrieval recall, in percent, is required?
variants.hint: Divide the target by the reader's rate.
variants.explanation: 0.81 / 0.90 = 0.90, so retrieval must supply accepted evidence for 90 percent of answerable questions.

mistakes.feedback: That multiplies 81 by 90 percent; the target is the product, so divide instead.
That subtracts the rates; the relation is multiplicative, not additive.

variants.title: Read the failure map
variants.context: Each metric and outcome bucket answers a different question: exact match is the strict answer contract, token F1 gives partial span credit, retrieval recall measures evidence coverage, and no-answer behavior tracks correct abstentions apart from unsupported answers.
variants.prompt: Match each metric to the question it answers.

pairs.label: Exact match
pairs.detail: After declared normalization, does the prediction equal at least one accepted alias?

pairs.label: Token F1
pairs.detail: How much do the normalized prediction and answer tokens overlap, with partial credit?

pairs.label: Retrieval recall
pairs.detail: Does at least one acceptable evidence unit appear in the retrieved top-k set?

pairs.label: No-answer behavior
pairs.detail: Are correct abstentions and unsupported answers tracked separately?

variants.hint: Two metrics score the answer text, one scores the evidence, and one scores the decision to answer.
variants.explanation: Exact match and token F1 score the answer under different strictness, retrieval recall scores evidence coverage, and no-answer behavior scores selective answering.

variants.title: Read the failure map
variants.context: Each metric and outcome bucket answers a different question: exact match is the strict answer contract, token F1 gives partial span credit, retrieval recall measures evidence coverage, and no-answer behavior tracks correct abstentions apart from unsupported answers.
variants.prompt: The pipeline diagnosis puts every question in exactly one bucket. Match each bucket to its definition.

pairs.label: Supported correct
pairs.detail: Accepted evidence was retrieved and the reader's answer matches an alias.

pairs.label: Retrieval miss
pairs.detail: No accepted evidence appeared in the retrieved set for an answerable question.

pairs.label: Reader error
pairs.detail: Accepted evidence was retrieved but the reader's answer does not match any alias.

pairs.label: Correct abstention
pairs.detail: The item was unanswerable and the system returned no answer.

pairs.label: Unsupported answer
pairs.detail: The system answered although the evidence did not contain support.

variants.hint: Ask two questions per bucket: did the evidence arrive, and was answering the right decision?
variants.explanation: The buckets partition outcomes by whether evidence arrived, whether the reader used it, and whether answering or abstaining was justified.

variants.title: Read the failure map
variants.context: Each metric and outcome bucket answers a different question: exact match is the strict answer contract, token F1 gives partial span credit, retrieval recall measures evidence coverage, and no-answer behavior tracks correct abstentions apart from unsupported answers.
variants.prompt: Match each line of the minimum production report to the failure it can reveal.

pairs.label: Retrieval recall at each declared k
pairs.detail: Evidence coverage that a reader cannot repair on its own.

pairs.label: Oracle-reader performance with gold evidence
pairs.detail: Reader quality when retrieval is removed from the equation.

pairs.label: Unsupported-answer rate
pairs.detail: Answers given without evidence to back them.

pairs.label: Over-refusal rate
pairs.detail: Answerable questions the system refused, hiding behind a strong no-answer score.

variants.hint: Each line isolates one stage or one decision so the others cannot hide it.
variants.explanation: The report separates evidence coverage, reader quality with gold evidence, unsupported answering, and over-refusal so an aggregate gain cannot mask a regression.

variants.title: Match the contract to the claim
variants.context: The evidence contract must match the product claim. Closed-book, retrieved-evidence, and supplied-passage results must not blend into one score, null answers stay in the denominator, and a high no-answer score is not proof of usefulness.
variants.prompt: To make Natural Questions easier to run, an engineer filters out every item annotated as having no supported answer and reports the short-answer score on the rest. What is the problem?
options: None; null items add noise and the short-answer task is what matters.
Removing null answers from the denominator creates an easier task and hides abstention behavior.
Only long answers should be reported, so the short-answer score is the wrong metric.
optionFeedback: Null answers are part of the benchmark's decision structure, not noise.
Keeping nulls in the denominator preserves the task's abstention component.
Long and short answers are both valid views; the error is dropping the null cases.
variants.hint: What happens to the denominator when a whole answer type disappears?
variants.explanation: Keep null answers in the denominator; filtering them creates an easier task and erases the no-answer decision the benchmark tests.

variants.title: Match the contract to the claim
variants.context: The evidence contract must match the product claim. Closed-book, retrieved-evidence, and supplied-passage results must not blend into one score, null answers stay in the denominator, and a high no-answer score is not proof of usefulness.
variants.prompt: A team evaluates only the reader on gold Natural Questions pages and describes the result as end-to-end search quality. What is the correct label for that experiment?
options: A reader-only measurement with gold evidence, not end-to-end search.
End-to-end search, since Natural Questions is built from real search queries.
A closed-book recall measurement, since no retrieval ran.
optionFeedback: Retrieval was never part of the evaluated system, so the claim cannot include it.
The dataset's origin does not make a reader-only run into a retrieval evaluation.
The reader received a gold page, so this is passage reading, not closed-book recall.
variants.hint: Which stages actually ran in the evaluated system?
variants.explanation: Do not call a reader-only experiment end-to-end search unless retrieval is part of the evaluated system; label it as reader quality on supplied evidence.

variants.title: Match the contract to the claim
variants.context: The evidence contract must match the product claim. Closed-book, retrieved-evidence, and supplied-passage results must not blend into one score, null answers stay in the denominator, and a high no-answer score is not proof of usefulness.
variants.prompt: A new model raises the correct-abstention rate from 60 to 95 percent, and the aggregate score improves. Before calling that a win, what must the report also show?
options: The token F1 score on the unanswerable subset.
The exact match score on the answerable subset and the over-refusal rate.
The number of training examples the new model saw.
optionFeedback: Token F1 on unanswerable items has no span to overlap; the risk is over-refusal on answerable ones.
Abstaining more can raise the aggregate while refusing answerable questions; coverage must be visible.
Training set size does not reveal whether the system became less useful.
variants.hint: How could a system get better at refusing while getting worse for users?
variants.explanation: A high no-answer score can hide blanket refusal; report answer coverage and over-refusal beside it.
